output:
I’ve been meaning to write this properly for a while, and I’d rather tell everyone at once than have the news travel round the family in bits.

The house in Glenmore, near Oughterard, is sold. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it closes on 15 January 2027.

I’m sorry that some of you heard about it from someone else before I’d told you myself. Declan, I’m especially sorry you found out from Gráinne on WhatsApp, rather than from me. You rang at two in the morning your time, and I know how hurt and angry you were. You said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back that I shouldn’t have. I regret that, and I regret not speaking to you before agreeing the sale. I’m not going to pretend I handled it well.

But I want to be honest about the decision, too. I’m sorry for how you found out; I’m not sorry that I’ve decided to sell.

Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin, built the house in 1931. Tom grew up there, and it became part of our life together. He proposed to me in the haggard behind it in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching. There was nothing grand about the occasion, but I remember it as clearly as if it were yesterday.

I remember the children learning to swim in the lake below the house. Declan, you refused to come out until your lips were blue. I can still hear the arguments about getting you dried and warmed up. There are photographs, small moments and family stories tied to that place, and I know we don’t all carry them in quite the same way.

Tom died in March 2024. Since then I’ve driven out every fortnight, about forty minutes each way, to air the house and check the pipes. At first, it felt like something I could manage. I thought I was looking after the place for all of us, and perhaps that was true for a while. But over the best part of two years, I’ve come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house.

The practical side has become harder, too. In September, Ó Flaithearta’s survey found that the roof needs work on the slates and back chimney. The quote was €38,000. There’s damp in the back bedroom, and the septic tank needs replacing before the house could be sold to anyone. Those are not small jobs, and I can’t take them on.

There is another part I haven’t told you until now. Last February, I slipped on the back step in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up. I didn’t tell anyone. I suppose I didn’t want to worry you, and I may have been hoping that if I kept quiet about it, it would feel like less of a warning. It doesn’t. Since the fall, I’ve been afraid of being alone at the house. I can’t go on maintaining it as I have been.

I know this is difficult news, particularly because the house means so much more than its roof, pipes and tank. It’s a family place, and I understand why it can feel as if selling it is the same as giving something away that can’t be replaced. But Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I’ve thought about that a lot. The people buying it are a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house, not use it as a holiday let. That mattered to me.

There were higher offers in the summer from people in Dublin. I chose the lower offer from the Joyces on purpose. The price was fair, but this wasn’t just about getting the most money. I wanted the house to go to people who meant to make a home there.

The Joyces have said the family can come out and walk the land any time. I’m glad of that. It won’t be ours in the same way after the sale, but the land and the memories won’t suddenly disappear. I hope, in time, there will be children in that house again, making their own memories.

I’m keeping some things. The dresser is going to Úna’s. Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign will stay with the family, too. I know those are only objects, but they hold stories, and I want them to have a place with us.

Before the house is cleared, I’d like us to have one more family day there. If you can, come out on Sunday 13 December. We’ll have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because it is December in Galway and the ground will be what it is. I’d love to see whoever can make it, and there’s no pressure on anyone who can’t. We can walk the land, sit in the house and be together there one more time before the move.

Declan, I know you’re hurt, and I understand why. I’m not angry with you. I love you, and the door is open whenever you want to talk. I’m not asking you to agree with me or to feel differently about the house. I only want you to hear this from me, and to know that I didn’t make the decision because Tom, or any of you, matters less to me.

The sale closes on 15 January 2027. I wanted everyone to have that date from me, so nobody has to hear it second-hand again.

I’ll see some of you on the 13th, I hope. In the meantime, I’m thinking of you all, near and far.
